displayQuote: A friend is someone who knows the song in your heart and can sing it back to you when you have forgotten the words

meta.title: Who really said "A friend knows the song in your heart"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not C.S. Lewis, not Shania Twain. The oldest credit we can document is 'Donna Roberts', a name attached to a shorter version in print by 2007 — and nobody has ever identified her. Honest answer: unknown.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A friend knows the song in your heart'?
meta.ogDescription: A wedding-and-eulogy staple with no source. Lewis never wrote it; the only credit with any paper behind it is a woman nobody can identify.

answer.label: Unknown — and the one named candidate is untraceable
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · a shorter version credited to ‘Donna Roberts’ in print by 2007
answer.sourceLine: There is no source. It is not in C.S. Lewis — not in The Four Loves, where he wrote at length about friendship, and not in his other books, letters or talks. Shania Twain is credited only because she has repeated it. The oldest credit with anything behind it is ‘Donna Roberts’, attached to a shorter wording in a 2007 book — and no one has ever established who she is.

source.excerpt: A friend knows the song in my heart and sings it to me when my memory fails.
trail: The C.S. Lewis end is a dead end, and it has been checked properly. Researchers who work through the Lewis corpus report that the line appears nowhere in The Four Loves or anywhere else in his published writing, and they name Donna Roberts as the credit it displaced the Lewis check ↗.

The oldest instance anyone has produced is the shorter first-person version above, credited to Donna Roberts in Lisa J. Copen’s Beyond Casseroles: 505 Ways to Encourage a Chronically Ill Friend (2007). That is a book repeating a credit, not a source — but it is the earliest paper trail there is.

‘Donna Roberts’ herself is a ghost. Quotation databases list her with no dates, no nationality, no book and no biography — only this saying. We have found nothing that identifies her, and we are not going to invent it.
source.excerptNote: The shorter, first-person wording — the oldest form we can document, and noticeably plainer than the version on wedding programmes. ‘When my memory fails’ is a sickbed line, not a toast.

sourceLink.text: Essential C.S. Lewis — it is not his

source.rightsNote: We cannot state the rights position, because we cannot state the author — and that is the honest answer rather than a convenient one. If ‘Donna Roberts’ is a real modern writer, the line is her copyrighted text and is not free for commercial reuse; if it is a folk saying, it belongs to nobody. Both are live possibilities, so treat it as protected until someone identifies her: quote it in a speech or a card, but do not build a product on it. What you should not do is print ‘C.S. Lewis’ underneath — a dead author with a famous name is exactly the fig leaf this saying has been wearing. This is not legal advice.

author.name: C.S. Lewis
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned to
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on C.S. Lewis
author.metaLine: 1898–1963 · Oxford and Cambridge scholar, author of The Four Loves
author.bio: Clive Staples Lewis wrote an entire book about the kinds of love, The Four Loves, with a long section on friendship — which is exactly why unsourced friendship aphorisms drift towards him. He is warm, quotable, dead, and famous enough that his name settles an argument. The line on this page is not in The Four Loves, not in his letters, and not in anything else he published; the resemblance is one of temperature, not of text.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Read at a wedding, read at a funeral, embroidered on a cushion — and nobody knows who wrote it. Every famous name attached to it collapses on contact, and the one obscure name that survives cannot be traced to a person.

items.why: Absent from The Four Loves and from the rest of the published corpus. Lewis is one of the most thoroughly indexed authors of the twentieth century; if it were there, it would have been found the check ↗.
She has quoted it, which is how quote sites now list her as its author. That is the standard mechanism by which a famous person acquires someone else’s sentence.
Attached to the shorter version in a 2007 book and to the long version in every database since. No dates, no publications, no biography anywhere. It is the best lead available and it goes nowhere.

The Norwegian writer (1851–1924) is widely credited with ‘to love a person is to learn the song in their heart and sing it to them when they have forgotten.’ Nobody cites which of his works it comes from, so it cannot yet do the job of an origin.

misattribution.truthLine: Unknown. Not Lewis, not Twain — and ‘Donna Roberts’ is a credit, not a person we can find the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It describes something friendship actually does and most definitions miss: not shared interests or long history, but being reminded who you are on a day you cannot remember. That is why it turns up at weddings and at funerals, which are the two occasions when people need it said out loud.

The music image also lets you say something enormous without embarrassment. ‘You keep my sense of myself alive’ is unsayable at a microphone; a song you have forgotten the words to is sayable, and everyone understands it.
context.detailsSummary: Why an anonymous saying still gets a famous name
detailsBody: A quote read aloud at a funeral wants an author; ‘anonymous’ sounds like the speaker did not do the reading. So a name gets supplied.
The name supplied is nearly always someone the audience already trusts on this subject — which, for friendship in English, means C.S. Lewis.
The shorter 2007 version is a sickbed line: a friend singing to someone whose memory is failing. The wedding version is smoother and less specific, which is usually the direction of travel.
‘Unknown’ is not a failure here. It is the correct answer, and it is more useful than a confident wrong one you might print on something.
context.pull: Read at weddings and at funerals — the two times people need it said out loud.
